Reveal: two ways to set the bound

items.item: A bounded dedup window is not a weaker version of unbounded dedup — it is a different, explicit guarantee ('duplicates within this bound are caught') that a system can actually afford to provide, unlike the unbounded version.

at.step: Reveal: forgotten on purpose

items.item: A wall-clock TTL and a watermark bound solve the same memory problem but fail differently under skew: a TTL can evict an id too early if a producer is delayed, while a watermark bound tracks the stream's own actual progress instead.

at.step: Reveal: two ways to set the bound

items.item: A Bloom filter's error is asymmetric by construction, not by tuning — bits can only be set, never cleared, so a false negative is structurally impossible regardless of how the filter is sized.

at.step: Reveal: one-directional, and measured

items.item: The false-positive rate is a dial, not a fixed cost — a larger bit array or more hash functions measurably lowers it, at the price of more memory per filter, the same space-versus-accuracy trade this topic's hook already set up.

at.step: Reveal: one-directional, and measured

items.item: A deterministic id only works when the derivation is actually deterministic — any non-deterministic input folded into it (a timestamp, a random value) breaks the exact same way non-deterministic processing breaks idempotent-upsert in the previous topic.

at.step: Reveal: idempotence, propagated one hop further

items.item: This topic's mechanism is strictly an application-level fallback — it exists because not every pipeline has a Kafka transaction or a two-phase-commit sink available, not because those mechanisms are insufficient where they do exist.

at.step: Setup: the same idea, one level up

items.item: The toy TTLDedupStore, TinyBloomFilter, and deterministic_id are deliberately simplified standalone models, not ports of any production dedup system, and the Bloom filter's measured false-positive rate is this run's own number, not a cited constant.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: Remembering an event id and remembering a derived event's deterministic id are the exact same mechanism applied twice in a row — the second application doesn't need any new machinery, only a new, equally deterministic id to feed it.

at.step: Reveal: idempotence, propagated one hop further

items.item: A dedup window's stated bound is itself part of the system's correctness contract — an operator who doesn't know the bound can't reason about when a duplicate might slip through, which is why naming it explicitly matters as much as choosing it.

Choosing between a TTL and a watermark bound is itself a smaller instance of a pattern that recurs throughout this chapter: trading a wall-clock guarantee for a stream-relative one whenever the stream's own progress is the more meaningful measure.
